::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: In psychology, and especially psycholinguistics and reading research, universality has been a central issue for decades.

text.text: Frost proposes that finding language-independent universalities in reading behaviour would be required for meaningful cross-linguistic modelling of language processing, thus human eye movement behaviour during reading.
Previously identified language-independent features mostly concern fixation durations and landing positions of saccades.

Among others, cross-linguistic similarities have been shown for landing positions in equal-length texts (Parshina et al., 2024), viewing durations of words (Siegelman et al., 2022), effects of word length and frequency on fixation durations and word skipping rates (Kuperman et al., 2024; Sui et al., 2023; Zdorova et al., 2023), and effects of word count, frequency, and length on sentence reading times (Liversedge et al., 2016 (Liversedge et al., , 2024)).

text.text: Furthermore, a non-linguistic universality in human eye movement behaviour is that eye movements do not directly land on targets when multiple stimuli are presented in the peripheral field of view (Coren & Hoenig, 1972; Findlay, 1982).

text.text: Thus, the goals of this investigation are (1) replicating the results of power-law behaviour for eye movements for the six original languages with further empirical data and (2) investigating whether the finding of power-law behaviour in relative saccade lengths can be generalised to further languages.

A successful extension of the results would provide further empirical evidence that the PDF of relative saccade lengths might constitute a universality in human eye movement behaviour.
If relative saccade lengths also observe powerlaw behaviour, this would indicate that adjustments of saccade lengths during reading follow optimal search behaviour.

text.text: For each language, the fits of the four different distributions can be compared via ΔAIC.
By definition, the best-fitting distribution with the lowest AIC has a ΔAIC of zero.
For any other distribution, ΔAIC is defined as the difference between the respective distribution's AIC and the AIC of the best-fitting distribution.
According to established interpretations, a ΔAIC less or equal to 2 suggests substantial evidence that a distribution fits the empirical data as well as the best-fitting distribution.
If ΔAIC is greater than 10, the evidence for a comparably good fit is negligible.
Note that the interpretation of ΔAIC does not depend on the absolute AIC scores since subtracting two AIC scores removes scaling constants from ΔAIC.

text.text: First, we aimed to replicate the original study's results, which cover Danish, Dutch, English, Estonian, Hebrew, Russian (Fabian, 2025).

text.text: As data, we use the eye-tracking data of MECO for the respective six languages.
Our results show that the PDFs of relative saccade lengths above 1 follow a power-law distribution for each of the original study's six languages.
There is virtually no empirical evidence supporting the three alternative distributions gamma, exponential, and lognormal.
Thus, we can confirm the original study's results with our replication based on new empirical evidence.
However, for the six languages, our results show an average power-law coefficient α of 2.04 (SD = 0.09), compared to 1.85 (SD = 0.08) reported in the original study.
We suspect this discrepancy arises from the MECO corpus' smaller amount of data for each language.
While the original study ensured each dataset contains at least 75,000 observations, only two of the six languages, English and Russian, meet this criterion in the MECO corpus.
Since large relative saccade lengths only occur with a probability of less than 0.1%, small datasets might not contain any observations of some larger relative saccade lengths.
Since the fitting algorithms consider all bins of relative saccade lengths, bins without any observation yield steeper estimated slopes, thus higher power-law coefficients α.
Therefore, smaller datasets without any observations of some large relative saccade lengths yield systematically higher power-law coefficients.
Second, we investigated whether the results for the six languages from the original study can be generalised to further languages.
MECO provides eye-tracking data for 15 languages beyond the originally investigated six.
For each of these 15 languages, the results show the power-law distribution fits the empirical PDF of relative saccade lengths above 1 best.
Empirical support for the three alternative distributions is indicated as negligible.
Hence, our results show the findings of the previously investigated six languages can be generalised to 21 languages in total.

This generalisation includes two non-alphabetic languages (Chinese, Hindi), two alphabetic languages with non-Latin scripts (Korean, Mongolian), and traditional Mongolian as a language that is read vertically.
Thus, the data indicate that the PDF of relative saccade lengths above 1 follows a power-law distribution during reading, regardless of the text's language.
With these two findings, this study contributes new empirical evidence that the PDF of relative saccade lengths might represent a universality in human eye movement behaviour.
Furthermore, the results show an average power-law coefficient α of 2.06 (SD = 0.17) for all 21 languages analysed.
Thus, the slope of the relative saccade length PDF is close to 2, which has been suggested optimal for search behaviour (Viswanathan et al., 1999).

text.text: While previous research does not consistently observe power-law behaviour for absolute saccade lengths (Bogartz & Staub, 2012; Brockmann & Geisel, 2000; Kelty-Stephen & Mirman, 2013; Stephen et al., 2009; Stephen & Mirman, 2010), this finding suggests an optimal or near-optimal adjustment process for saccade lengths during reading.

text.text: As relative saccade lengths capture relations between subsequent saccades, the results indicate that the search for the best-fitting relation between saccade lengths is near-optimal.
This finding provides a novel insight into human saccade planning since cross-linguistic influences remained largely unknown.
Relative saccade length PDFs appear as a stable statistical property in reading behaviour, describing eye movement behaviour independent of the language being read.
Thus, our study provides further empirical evidence that relative saccade length PDFs might constitute a universality in reading behaviour, as was theoretically proposed and demanded by Frost (2012).

text.text: Despite the successful replication and generalisation, this study has a few limitations.
First, although 21 languages represent a considerable extension from the previously analysed six languages, the vast majority of world languages remains unexplored.
Future studies could collect data from further underrepresented languages and generalise the findings of our analyses further.
Such extensions could show whether relative saccade length PDFs constitute a stable statistical property or even a universality in reading behaviour.
Second, for the six originally investigated languages, the average power-law coefficient of 2.04 estimated in this study slightly deviates from the 1.85 estimated in the original study.

We suspect this deviation stems from the fact that the, at least for our purposes, rather small datasets contained in MECO lead to systematically higher power-law coefficients than the large datasets analysed in the original study.
Larger datasets would be needed to ensure no systematic differences arise from the process of distribution fitting.

Since the aim of this study is to investigate power-law behaviour during reading for various languages, we leave analyses focusing on the exact replication of power-law coefficients with larger datasets to future research.
Third, our statements regarding empirical support for the possible universality of relative saccade length PDFs only concern reading behaviour.

To provide empirical support for visual search and scene perception, which were also analysed in the original study introducing relative saccade lengths (Fabian, 2025), further studies with more empirical data are needed.

text.text: In summary, this study confirms previous results regarding the power-law behaviour of eye movements during reading for six languages and shows that the findings can be extended to a total of 21 languages.
Eye movements during reading seem to share a statistical regularity, regardless of the text's language.
In contrast to the established differences between reading behaviour for different languages, the power-law-shaped tail of the relative saccade length PDF appears as a unifying statistical property.
This statistical property indicates that the adjustments of human eye movement lengths could be optimal independent of viewing context.
We hope this study contributes to establishing a common ground in human eye movement behaviour.
This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.
The empirical PDF of relative saccade lengths above 1 is fitted best by the power-law distribution for each of the 21 languages analysed, as well as the traditional and simplified Chinese script.
In each case, the gamma distribution fits the empirical data second best.
However, ΔAIC compared to the power-law is greater than 10,000 for the three other distributions for each language, indicating negligible evidence for a comparable fit.
Thus, for all languages analysed, the power-law distribution is the best-fitting distribution while gamma, exponential, and lognormal distributions achieve considerably worse fits.
For the power-law distributions, we estimate two parameters: (1) the power-law coefficient α which describes the distribution's slope and (2) the shift parameter.
Since the shift parameter is only introduced to ensure optimal fitting and does not represent distributional characteristics, we only report the results for the power-law coefficient α here.
We find that the power-law coefficient α is 2.06 (SD = 0.17) across all 21 languages, and 2.04 (SD = 0.09) for the six languages analysed in the original study (Fabian, 2025).
